thread.title: You’re not alone: Hedge fund manager Steven Cohen is suffering in the stock market too

author: Inan Dogan
title: You’re not alone: Hedge fund manager Steven Cohen is suffering in the stock market too
text:
Billionaire Steven Cohen is among the most famous hedge fund managers in the world. His SAC Capital is said to have returned 30% annually for more than 20 years since its inception in 1992. His net worth is more than $12 billion, and he made this money mostly by buying and selling stocks.
Earlier this month, Cohen disclosed owning 8.2% of SunOpta Inc. STKL, +1.92% and SunOpta’s stock promptly jumped as much as 7% and trading volume doubled following the disclosure. Was that an appropriate response for this kind of disclosure? Should investors react differently when Cohen discloses a large position?
Most of the time financial media report the changes in hedge funds’ positions, but they don’t tell us what these moves really mean. For example, in May 2016 a major financial news website reported that Jason Karp’s Tourbillon sent a letter to SunOpta urging it to sell the stock. The article mentioned that SunOpta’s shares jumped 27% after the disclosure of the activist campaign but didn’t give any indications about whether investors should follow Tourbillon into SunOpta based on the historical performance of Tourbillon’s stock picks.
That’s why we at Insider Monkey analyze the performance of historical stock picks of equity hedge funds, determine their strengths and weaknesses, and try to identify the best stocks to go long and short based on this analysis. Interestingly, this approach generated better returns than most hedge funds. Our flagship long strategy returned 71.8% since its inception in May 2014 vs. a 46.6% gain for the S&P 500 ETF SPY, +0.77% Our flagship short strategy’s picks lost 34.7% since we started sharing them in February 2017 in an up market where the S&P 500 ETF gained 12.3%. (Read the details here. )
So if you have any doubts about whether it makes sense to analyze hedge funds’ historical stock picks and base trades on the findings, we can assure you that there is some persistence in hedge funds’ returns. However, this approach doesn’t always lead to success, as some hedge funds may experience dramatic reversals in their performance for various reasons. In this article we are going to present one of these high-profile cases.
Cohen’s scandal You may remember that Cohen’s fund was involved in an insider-trading scandal in 2012. After several of Cohen’s employees were found guilty of illegal insider trading, the fund pleaded guilty as well, and it was hit with a record $1.8 billion fine. Although Cohen wasn’t charged with illegal insider trading, he was banned from managing outside money for two years on the basis that he failed to appropriately supervise his subordinates.
Hence, in 2016 Steve Cohen was forced to close down SAC Capital Advisors, but two years prior to the official closure, he spun off Point72 Asset Management. He was running this new fund as a family office waiting for the ban to expire, which finally happened in January of this year. Even before the ban was lifted, Point72 Asset Management was doing well. It managed around $11 billion in assets and generated a return of 15.5% in 2015.
This year started well for Cohen, as he has managed to raise around $5 billion since his Point72 Asset Management opened to outside investors. The fund gained around 10% through September. Unfortunately, the positive trend reversed in the fourth quarter, and the fund generated losses of 2.8% in October and 4.3% in November. This means that Point72 Asset Management is slightly up this year, similar to 2017, when the fund ended almost flat.
It seems that Cohen has high hopes for his fund’s future operations as he has been working on establishing a team of professionals. In recent months, he employed managers from Balyasny Asset Management and also hired staff from Morgan Stanley’s electronic trading desk. He was also planning to raise money in Britain, but somewhere in the middle of the year, it was reported that the U.K. regulator has blocked his fund from raising capital.
Replicating returns We downloaded Cohen’s 13F filings covering the 1999-2017 period. Those are quarterly filings that show Cohen’s stock holdings in U.S. stocks at the end of each quarter. Our goal here isn’t to replicate Cohen’s actual returns but to find pockets of intelligence in Cohen’s portfolio where he and his portfolio managers historically demonstrate strong stock-picking ability. We won’t be able to capture returns that are attributable to Cohen’s trading skills where he goes in and out of stocks in a short period of time. However, we are going to be able to capture the returns from most of Cohen’s long-term-oriented investments.
The table below summarizes the average monthly returns for several market-cap brackets of Cohen’s 13F portfolio:
As you can see, the entire 13F portfolio was able to beat the market by an average of 51 basis points per month between 1999 and 2007. This is the period where Steve Cohen still had his mojo and was actually generating 20%-plus annual gains. Our approach is to capture some of the excess returns generated by Cohen. You will also notice that Cohen’s 13F portfolio was able to outperform the market in all market-cap brackets we used covering the 1999-2007 period. His top five mid-cap stock picks outperformed the market by more than 15 percentage points annually.
Things slowed between 2008 and 2013, but Cohen’s 13F portfolio still managed to beat the market in all market-cap brackets. Overall, Cohen’s 13F portfolio managed to beat the market by 21 basis points per month during that period.
Underperformance Our results indicate that Cohen lost his mojo after he converted his fund into a family office. Between 2014 and 2017, Cohen’s 13F portfolio underperformed the market by 34 basis points per month. That’s a reversal of 85 basis points per month compared with the 1999-2007 period. None of the market-cap brackets in Cohen’s 13F portfolio was able to beat the market between 2014 and 2017. His top five mid-cap stocks actually lost an average of 18 basis points per month in a market that delivered an average monthly return of nearly 1%.
How did this happen? First, Cohen’s portfolio managers traded relatively freely prior to 2014 and a few of them crossed the line. It looks like illegal insider trading and gains tied to these transactions stopped in the past five years. Second, several talented managers left the firm and launched their own funds. For example, Cohen’s star portfolio manager Gabriel Plotkin generated a gain of 47% in his first year after leaving SAC Capital. Plotkin was managing around $1.5 billion at that time. If he stayed with Cohen, he might have generated those returns on behalf of Cohen.
Third, the days of star traders generating 30% annual returns are pretty much over. Stan Druckenmiller, who generated 30% annual returns for 30 years, acknowledged this fact in a recent video interview . Cohen’s returns were on a downward trend even before he converted his fund into a family office. Most investors know that it is easier to generate larger returns with a smaller portfolio. Cohen has been managing a much smaller portfolio in recent years, yet its returns are almost flat in the past couple of years. Having an extra $5 billion to invest won’t make it easier to generate large returns.
When I look at Cohen’s five biggest new positions in his latest 13F filing, I see Qualcomm QCOM, -0.05% Netflix NFLX, +1.45% Apple AAPL, -0.02% PVH PVH, +1.51% and A.O. Smith AOS, +2.18% Netflix is down 28% in the fourth quarter, and Apple is down 26%. The five picks lost an average of 25% since the beginning of October. When I look at the recent performance of Cohen’s stock picks, I simply don’t see any evidence of how he can start generating meaningful outperformance in a world that’s now dominated by algorithms and passive investing.
Inan Dogan , PhD, is the director of research at Insider Monkey .
